title: Agent-Based Modeling: Worlds Within Worlds
gist: A Santa Fe Institute history of agent-based modeling (ABM), from Manhattan Project cellular automata and the SFI Artificial Stock Market to data-driven housing-bubble models adopted by central banks and a COVID-19 ABM that forecast UK value added at -22.1% versus a -21.5% outcome (Bank of England ~-30%). It argues surging compute, data availability and machine learning are finally making an 'economy under glass' feasible, with central bank ABMs and policy labs as the next frontier.

insights.claim: Agent-based models build systems bottom-up from individual agents and their rules, capturing emergent, non-equilibrium behavior that top-down equation-based economic models assume away to keep the math clean.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Models that assume equilibrium systematically miss bubbles, crashes and regime shifts that drive tail risk in portfolios.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, something like a traditional economics model assumes away such complexity to make the math clean.

insights.claim: The Santa Fe Artificial Stock Market, built in the early 1990s with learning trader-agents that test and switch rules, naturally produced bubbles, crashes and persistent volatility rather than stable equilibria.
insights.speaker: Blake LeBaron
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous, adaptive agents are sufficient to generate realistic market turmoil, supporting the view that volatility clustering and crashes are endogenous.
insights.quote: It is hard to get the SFI Stock Market to not crash. And that means you get pretty realistic markets with bubbles, crashes, and persistent volatility.

insights.claim: Standard economic modelers assume supercapable, always-rational agents and hunt for stable equilibria, whereas real humans struggle to make optimal choices under complexity and change their minds.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Investment frameworks built on rational-expectations assumptions may underweight behavioral, strategy-switching dynamics.
insights.quote: Most standard economic modelers look for regularities. Assuming agents are supercapable and always make rational decisions, they develop mathematical equations to hunt for equilibria

insights.claim: Brian Arthur's 1994 El Farol Bar Problem showed that strange collective phenomena arise when agents try to predict other agents' crowd-avoiding behavior, and was taken up by game theorists, physicists and financiers.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Reflexive crowding dynamics are a useful lens for crowded trades and positioning reversals.

insights.claim: Robert Axelrod's computerized Prisoner's Dilemma tournaments found that the winning strategy was to cooperate first and then play tit-for-tat, showing simple computation could represent cooperation and betrayal.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Repeated-game dynamics inform how cartels, alliances and competitors sustain or break cooperation.
insights.quote: The unexpected winner: cooperate first, then follow a tit-for-tat strategy.

insights.claim: Schelling's segregation model showed that segregated neighborhoods can form from only a slight preference to live near similar people, even without policies such as redlining.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Small individual preferences can aggregate into large spatial sorting effects relevant to real estate and urban demand.

themes.theme: Housing-bubble ABMs and central bank adoption

insights.claim: Around 2014, Axtell, Farmer, Geanakoplos, Howitt and others built an ABM combining scraped Washington, D.C.-area county housing data with IRS and private mortgage data that correctly reproduced the dynamics of the housing bubble and crash.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Data-rich ABMs can replicate credit-driven housing cycles, a tool for gauging mortgage and real-estate risk.
insights.quote: They discover that they can bake all that information into an ABM that correctly details the dynamics of the housing market bubble and crash.

insights.claim: Central banks in England, Canada, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy, Spain, Hungary and France, plus the European Central Bank, adapted the housing-market-bubble ABM for their own countries.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Macroprudential housing policy (e.g. lending limits) in these jurisdictions is increasingly informed by agent-based simulations.

insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Regulators exploring ABMs for financial stability may shift stress-testing toward non-equilibrium contagion scenarios.

insights.claim: The 2008 financial crisis exposed failures and vulnerabilities of traditional economic models, pushing economists to search for new approaches including ABMs.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Crisis-driven model failures create demand for alternative modeling methods in macro and risk management.
insights.quote: In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, which illuminates the failures and vulnerabilities of traditional economic models, economists find themselves searching for new approaches.

insights.claim: A COVID-19 ABM by Doyne Farmer, Penny Mealy, R. Maria del Rio-Chanona and collaborators forecast a -22.1% fall in UK value added for April-June 2020 versus October-December 2019, against a real outcome of -21.5% and a Bank of England forecast of about -30%.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Production-network ABMs outperformed a central bank's shock forecast, suggesting value in such models for nowcasting abrupt supply/demand shocks.
insights.quote: Real life: −21.5%ABM forecast: −22.1%Bank of England forecast: ~−30%

insights.claim: The COVID ABM was built partly from analysts' ratings of how important each industry is to the functioning of every other industry, capturing supply-chain interdependencies under lockdown.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Inter-industry dependency mapping is a practical approach to estimating second-order shock propagation across sectors.

insights.claim: Traditional pandemic-era forecasts were farther off because most assume the economy is in equilibrium and struggle to capture how people and companies rapidly adjust behavior over time.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: During regime breaks, equilibrium-based consensus forecasts may be systematically biased, creating opportunities for differentiated views.
insights.quote: One reason is because most such models assume the economy is in equilibrium, an assumption the pandemic shatters.

insights.claim: The UK government implemented some of the ABM's recommendations, such as closing customer-facing industries while keeping upstream industries open, as it emerged from lockdown.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: ABM outputs have directly shaped sector-level policy decisions with market consequences.

themes.theme: Public health as ABM's first policy success

insights.claim: During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, the U.S. National Institutes of Health used a network of independent, data-fed infectious-disease ABMs, and federal, state and local health leaders acted on their forecasts.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Ensembles of independent models fed with large data produce more realistic predictions, a principle applicable to economic forecasting.
insights.quote: Comparing the results of independent ABMs fed with massive amounts of data leads to more realistic predictions.

insights.claim: In 2011 Ross Hammond announced the first ABM tackling a non-infectious public health issue (obesity), and ABM research went on to underpin reports used to craft FDA policy and shape USDA food recommendations.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Simulation-informed regulation can affect food and health-sector companies through policy channels.

insights.claim: By the early 2010s most real-world ABM applications were outside economics, because getting enough data on the right variables to make useful economic predictions was next to impossible.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Data availability, not method, was the binding constraint on economic ABMs, implying alternative data is the key enabler.
insights.quote: Getting enough data about the right variables to make useful economic predictions for policymakers is next to impossible.

themes.theme: Compute and data as the enabling curve

insights.claim: Peak supercomputer performance rose from about 3.4 MFLOPS in 1977 to 1.742 EFLOPS in 2024 and an estimated 2.198 EFLOPS as of June 2026.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Exponential compute growth keeps expanding the feasible scale of simulation-based economic and financial models.
insights.quote: 2.198 EFLOPS is the estimated computing power for the world’s most powerful computer as of June 2026.

insights.claim: Data availability exploded from punch-card-era archives to 186,476 datasets on Data.gov in 2016 and more than 31 million datasets on Google Dataset Search by 2020.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Public and alternative data growth is what lets ABMs be calibrated to real economies.
insights.locator: Government data moves online en masse

insights.claim: ABM research output grew from more than 50 new papers in 2002 to more than 900 new papers and over 24,000 citations in 2025.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Rapid academic growth signals ABMs moving from fringe to mainstream in policy and possibly industry modeling.

insights.so_what: Simulation-based macro forecasting could become a competitive edge for policymakers and investors with the data and compute to run it.

insights.claim: Stefani Crabtree's 2017 ABM of Ancestral Puebloans, tested across 36 scenarios against archaeological data spanning nearly 700 years, suggested small egalitarian communities gave way to hierarchical polities that broke up after climate changes.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Climate shocks can dissolve complex political structures, a historical analogue for climate-driven geopolitical risk.
